args.text: [lane-ibis] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System, the internet's address book) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to an old server that has moved or been retired, so services fail. (2) Slow recovery: if a site switches to a backup server during an outage, cached answers delay the switch for as long as they last. (3) Prolonged poisoning: if a false answer is cached, whether by attack or mistake, it keeps misdirecting users until it expires.

[lane-ibis] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail unpredictably, so a client often cannot tell whether its first request succeeded, and it must be able to try again safely. If a request is idempotent (repeating it gives the same result as doing it once), a retry cannot cause harm such as a double payment or a duplicate order.

[lane-ibis] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (a time-ordered universally unique identifier) as a primary key: (1) Larger keys: it takes more storage than a plain integer, so indexes and foreign keys grow and fewer entries fit in memory. (2) Leaked creation time: the first part encodes when the record was made, so anyone seeing the identifier can estimate that, and records created at the same moment have only loosely ordered keys. The upside is that its time ordering avoids the scattered index inserts of random UUIDs.

[lane-ibis] A write-ahead log (WAL) is a record of each change that a database writes to durable storage before it alters the main data files. If the system crashes, it replays this log to recover committed changes and discard unfinished ones, so no data is lost or left half-written.

[lane-ibis] (1) Pinning the client version keeps the results comparable: if the client changes between runs, any difference in speed could come from the client rather than the system being tested. (2) It makes the benchmark repeatable, so others can rerun it later and get the same setup, without unexpected changes from updates.

[lane-ibis] Backpressure is a way for a queue to tell the senders to slow down when the receivers cannot keep up, for example by refusing new items or making senders wait. This stops the queue growing without limit, which would otherwise use up memory and make delays worse for everyone.

[lane-ibis] A cron job (a scheduled task) can run twice when (1) two servers carry the same schedule, or (2) a slow earlier run is still going when the next one starts. Guard: take a lock before working, so a second copy sees the lock and exits.

[lane-ibis] A tombstone is a marker stored in place of a deleted item, so every copy in a replicated store learns the item was removed. Without it, a copy that missed the delete could send the old value back and bring the item to life again. Tombstones are cleared away after a set time.

[lane-ibis] Two signs a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no change in between, so rerunning it gives different results. (2) The failures depend on things outside the code, such as timing, test order, shared data or network delays, and they often vanish when the test is run alone.

[lane-ibis] A lease-based lock gives a holder the lock only until a set time. Clock skew means the holder's clock and the lock service's clock disagree, so the holder may think it still owns the lock after the service has expired it and given it to someone else. Two holders then work at once, which the lock was meant to prevent.
